title: Egerton (Cairo) → Gordon (Khartoum), numeric cipher telegram that Gordon could not read: 23 six-digit groups printed in Hake's edition
correspondents: Egerton at Cairo (sender per Gordon's journal; the telegram itself is unsigned in the print) → General C. G. Gordon, Khartoum
shelfmark: Printed: A. E. Hake (ed.), The Journals of Major-Gen. C. G. Gordon, C.B., at Kartoum (London 1885), Book I, p. 50, footnote 67 (archive.org journalsmajorge00hakegoog; Gutenberg 49224). Original: Gordon's journal MS with the telegram pasted in, location not verified (British Library, unconfirmed)
folio_note: 23 groups of 6 digits, headed 'Cairo, August 30th, 10.30 P.M.', printed in full in the footnote; Gordon: 'Egerton's cipher telegram, which I cannot decipher'; a clear note written on its back is also printed
status: Seen on the printed page (page image of the archive.org scan, 14 Nov 2026) and in the OCR of two editions. Digits: 445737 905309 185115 417291 552676 792996 271381 511906 689363 945242 226739 648255 102037 626054 535222 672318 277535 134971 467430 203151 804960 483289 681510. No decipherment in the book: Gordon says Stewart took the cipher books. Plaintext may survive in the Foreign Office / Egypt papers (not searched). Not in the repo (known.py 445737, Khartoum, Egerton: no match). Not on DECODE (2 searches). Related and distinct: PRO 30/57/4/119 (Wolseley, 19 Oct 1884) is already in the catalogue; Durham SAD.250/1/550 (Gordon's Arabic-numeral note) is a lead of the north-east literature sweep.
why: A British Foreign Office numeric code of 1884 in use on the Khartoum line; Gordon's journal names two more such telegrams (Wolseley's and Nubar/Baring's) that he also could not read, so the code groups could be compared if the originals are found.

title: Papers of the Dutch passenger Prediger seized at the Cape, incl. a long letter in cypher: Governor Yonge to Dundas, secret
correspondents: Sir George Yonge, Governor of the Cape → Henry Dundas (enclosing Prediger's papers); the cypher letter's writer and addressee unknown
shelfmark: Printed: G. M. Theal, Records of the Cape Colony vol. III (1898), p. 387 (archive.org recordsofcapecol00thea_17, recordsofcapecol03theauoft); source: Cape Colony original correspondence copied from the Public Record Office, i.e. TNA CO 48 (volume not identified from the print)
folio_note: Theal: 'The Enclosures, excepting a long letter in cypher, are not now to be found.' Yonge: Prediger, 'pretending to go as a neutral Passenger to Batavia', had his papers seized, some in cypher, hidden in his baggage; Yonge sent him to England
status: Catalogue level (printed edition): the cypher letter survives among the Cape despatches, extent unknown, no decipherment mentioned. The repo's batavia1800 target is a cipher letter of 20 Nov 1800 to a C. J. Prediger at Batavia from the Raad der Aziatische Bezittingen (key rebuilt, simple 2-digit-grid substitution): same name and period, but identity of the two Predigers and any link between the systems is not established. Not on DECODE (3 searches: Prediger, Yonge, Cape of Good Hope). Not otherwise in the repo. Not viewed.
why: A Dutch colonial-council cipher captured on the way to Batavia, possibly in the same system as the solved batavia1800 letter, which would give a ready key.
